passages: [L1] For a future timelike $P$ with $m=m(P)>0$: $\gamma\ge1$, $E_n(P)=mc^2\gamma$, $q_n(P)=m\gamma w$, $g_p(q_n,q_n)=m^2c^2(\gamma^2-1)$ and $E_n^2=m^2c^4+c^2g_p(q_n,q_n)$ ([[lem-gr-observer-energy-momentum-identities]] clause 3, [[def-gr-observer-relative-energy-and-momentum]] clauses (a)-(b)).

[L2] Taylor's theorem with Lagrange remainder: if $f$ is $C^2$ on an interval containing $0$ and $z$, then $|f(z)-f(0)-f'(0)z|\le\tfrac12\sup_{0\le t\le z}|f''(t)|z^2$; if $f$ is $C^1$, then $|f(z)-f(0)|\le\sup_{0\le t\le z}|f'(t)|z$ ([[cor-taylor-lagrange-and-cauchy-remainders]], [[thm-mean-value-inequality-for-total-derivatives]], [[def-interval]]).

[L3] For $z<1$, the base $1-z$ is positive; the rational power defined by [[def-rational-power]] at exponent $-\tfrac12$ agrees with the corresponding real power ([[thm-real-power-agrees-with-rational-exponent]]). The real-power derivative formula $(y^\alpha)'=\alpha y^{\alpha-1}$ for $y>0$, applied at $\alpha=-\tfrac12$ and then $\alpha=-\tfrac32$, together with the chain and scalar rules ([[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]), gives $f(z)=(1-z)^{-1/2}\in C^2((-\infty,1))$ and $$f'(z)=\tfrac12(1-z)^{-3/2},\qquad f''(z)=\tfrac34(1-z)^{-5/2}.$$

1.1 (The relative speed and the Lorentz factor.) Combining $q_n=m\gamma w$ with $g_p(q_n,q_n)=m^2c^2(\gamma^2-1)$ from [L1] gives $m^2\gamma^2s^2=m^2c^2(\gamma^2-1)$, hence $\gamma^2(c^2-s^2)=c^2$; since $\gamma\ge1>0$ this reads $\gamma=(1-s^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, and the identity forces $s<c$ as well as $s^2/c^2=1-\gamma^{-2}$. [L1, algebra]

1.2 (Taylor bounds for the Lorentz factor.) Let $f(z):=(1-z)^{-1/2}$ on $[0,z_0]$ with $z_0<1$. By [L3] and [L2], $$|f(z)-1-\tfrac12z|\le\tfrac12\sup_{t\in[0,z_0]}|f''(t)|z^2=\tfrac38(1-z_0)^{-5/2}z^2,\qquad |f(z)-1|\le\sup_{t\in[0,z_0]}|f'(t)|z=\tfrac12(1-z_0)^{-3/2}z .$$ [L2, L3, algebra]

2.1 (Energy and momentum formulas.) By [L1] and step 1.1, $g_p(q_n,q_n)=m^2\gamma^2s^2$ and $\gamma>0$, so $|q_n(P)|=\sqrt{g_p(q_n,q_n)}=m\gamma s$; hence, with $E_n=mc^2\gamma$, $E_n(P)=mc^2(1-s^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$ and $|q_n(P)|=ms(1-s^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$. [step 1.1, L1, algebra]

3.1 (Energy expansion.) Substituting $z=s^2/c^2$ in the first bound of step 1.2 into $E_n=mc^2f(z)$ of step 2.1 gives $|E_n-mc^2-\tfrac12ms^2|\le mc^2\cdot\tfrac38(1-z_0)^{-5/2}(s^4/c^4)=\tfrac38(1-z_0)^{-5/2}ms^4/c^2$. [step 2.1, step 1.2, algebra]
3.2 (Momentum expansion.) Likewise $|q_n|=msf(z)$ by step 2.1, so $||q_n|-ms|=ms|f(z)-1|\le ms\cdot\tfrac12(1-z_0)^{-3/2}(s^2/c^2)=\tfrac12(1-z_0)^{-3/2}ms^3/c^2$. [step 2.1, step 1.2, algebra]
4.1 (Conclusion.) Step 2.1 gives the identities of the statement (including $s<c$), and steps 3.1 and 3.2 give the two uniform error bounds for $s\le v_0<c$. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 3.2, given] ∎

[L1] $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\sum_dg^{ad}(\partial_bg_{cd}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc})$ in the chart, and the components of the inverse metric satisfy $|\partial^\alpha g^{ab}(\varepsilon)|\le C_1/L^{|\alpha|}$ on the spacetime portion over $K$ for $|\alpha|\le2$, together with the sharp expansion $g^{ab}(\varepsilon)=\eta^{ab}-\eta^{ac}E_{cd}(\varepsilon)\eta^{db}+R^{ab}(\varepsilon)$ with $E=g(\varepsilon)-\eta$ and $|R^{ab}(\varepsilon)|\le C_1\varepsilon^2$, which in particular gives $|g^{ab}(\varepsilon)-\eta^{ab}|\le C_1\varepsilon$, $|g^{00}+1|\le C_1\varepsilon$, and $|g^{0i}(\varepsilon)|\le C_1\varepsilon^{3/2}$ ([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]], [[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]], [[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]], [[lem-gr-weak-field-admissibility-and-inverse-bounds]]).

[L2] The metric coefficients are pullbacks from $U$: $g_{00}=-(1+2\varepsilon\varphi)+r_{00}$, $g_{ij}=(1-2\varepsilon\varphi)\delta_{ij}+r_{ij}$, $g_{0i}=r_{0i}$; for spatial $i$, $|\partial_ir_{00}|+|\partial_ir_{jk}|\le C\varepsilon^2/L$, $|\partial_ir_{0j}|\le C\varepsilon^{3/2}/L$, and $|\partial_i\varphi|\le C/L$ on $K$, while all time derivatives of the pulled-back components vanish ([[def-gr-stationary-weak-field-data]] clause (a)).
[L3] Derivatives of sums and products obey the usual rules and component fields are smooth ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]).

1.1 (Derivative bounds of the metric components.) By [L2], for spatial $i$ one has $\partial_i\widetilde\Phi=\varepsilon c^2\partial_i\varphi$ and $|\partial_i\varphi|\le C/L$, so $|\partial_i g_{00}|\le2\varepsilon C/L+C\varepsilon^2/L\le C'\varepsilon/L$, $|\partial_i g_{jk}|\le C'\varepsilon/L$ and $|\partial_i g_{0j}|\le C\varepsilon^{3/2}/L$. All time derivatives of the metric components are zero by stationarity. [L2, algebra]

2.1 (The component with two lower zeros.) By [L1] and stationarity [L2], $\Gamma^i{}_{00}=\tfrac12g^{ia}(2\partial_0g_{a0}-\partial_ag_{00})=-\tfrac12g^{ia}\partial_ag_{00}=\tfrac12g^{ia}(2\partial_a\widetilde\Phi/c^2-\partial_ar_{00})$, since $\partial_ag_{00}=-2\varepsilon\partial_a\widetilde\varphi+\partial_ar_{00}=-2\partial_a\widetilde\Phi/c^2+\partial_ar_{00}$. Write $g^{ia}=\eta^{ia}+(g^{ia}-\eta^{ia})$ and use $\eta^{ia}\partial_a\widetilde\Phi=\partial_i\Phi$, because $i\ne0$ and the only nonzero entries of $\eta^{ia}$ with $i\ne0$ are the spatial $\delta^{ia}$: the first term gives $\partial_i\Phi/c^2$, while $|(g^{ia}-\eta^{ia})\partial_a\widetilde\Phi/c^2|\le C_1\varepsilon\cdot C\varepsilon/L$ by [L1] and [L2] and $|\tfrac12g^{ia}\partial_ar_{00}|\le\tfrac12C'C\varepsilon^2/L$; hence $|\Gamma^i{}_{00}-\partial_i\Phi/c^2|\le C_2\varepsilon^2/L$. [step 1.1, L1, L2, L3, algebra]

2.2 (The remaining components.) Again by [L1] and stationarity, $\Gamma^i{}_{0j}=\tfrac12g^{ia}(\partial_jg_{a0}-\partial_ag_{0j})$. Split the sum into $a=0$ and spatial $a=k$: the $a=0$ term is $\tfrac12g^{i0}\partial_jg_{00}$, bounded by $C'\varepsilon^{5/2}/L$ using [L1], [L2] and step 1.1; each spatial term $\tfrac12g^{ik}(\partial_jr_{k0}-\partial_kr_{0j})$ is bounded by $C'\varepsilon^{3/2}/L$ using [L1] and [L2]. These bounds are uniform in $p\in K$ and $0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_*$, and their finite sum gives $|\Gamma^i{}_{0j}|\le C_2\varepsilon^{3/2}/L$. Next, $\Gamma^i{}_{jk}=\tfrac12g^{ia}(\partial_jg_{ak}+\partial_kg_{aj}-\partial_ag_{jk})$; splitting off the explicit $\varphi$-terms leaves $\tfrac12g^{ia}(-2\varepsilon)(\delta_{ak}\partial_j\widetilde\varphi+\delta_{aj}\partial_k\widetilde\varphi-\delta_{jk}\partial_a\widetilde\varphi)$, whose absolute value is at most $C'\varepsilon/L$ by [L1] and [L2], while the $r$-terms contribute at most $C'\varepsilon^2/L$; hence $|\Gamma^i{}_{jk}|\le C_2\varepsilon/L$. For the components with upper index $0$, use the sharp inverse expansion of [L1], $g^{0a}=\eta^{0a}-\eta^{0c}E_{cd}\eta^{da}+R^{0a}$, with $|R^{0a}|\le C_1\varepsilon^2$: the inverse bounds in [L1] give $|g^{00}+1|\le C_1\varepsilon$, $|g^{0i}|\le C_1\varepsilon^{3/2}$ and $|g^{00}|\le C_1$. For $\Gamma^0{}_{00}=\tfrac12g^{0a}(2\partial_0g_{a0}-\partial_ag_{00})=-\tfrac12g^{0a}\partial_ag_{00}$ the $a=0$ term vanishes by stationarity and the $a=i$ term contributes at most $\tfrac12C'\varepsilon^{3/2}\cdot C'\varepsilon/L\le C_2\varepsilon^{5/2}/L$. For $\Gamma^0{}_{0j}=\tfrac12g^{0a}(\partial_jg_{a0}-\partial_ag_{0j})$ the $a=0$ term is $\tfrac12g^{00}\partial_jg_{00}$ with $|g^{00}|\le C_1$ and $|\partial_jg_{00}|\le C'\varepsilon/L$, and the $a=i$ term is $\tfrac12g^{0i}(\partial_jr_{i0}-\partial_ir_{0j})$ of size at most $C'\varepsilon^{3/2}\cdot C'\varepsilon^{3/2}/L\le C'\varepsilon^3/L$; hence $|\Gamma^0{}_{0j}|\le C_2\varepsilon/L$. Finally $\Gamma^0{}_{jk}=\tfrac12g^{0a}(\partial_jg_{ak}+\partial_kg_{aj}-\partial_ag_{jk})$: the $a=0$ term is $\tfrac12g^{00}(\partial_jr_{0k}+\partial_kr_{0j})$ of size at most $C_1C\varepsilon^{3/2}/L\le C'\varepsilon^{3/2}/L$, and the $a=i$ term is at most $C'\varepsilon^{3/2}\cdot C'\varepsilon/L\le C'\varepsilon^{5/2}/L$; hence $|\Gamma^0{}_{jk}|\le C_2\varepsilon^{3/2}/L$. [step 1.1, L1, L2, L3, algebra]

3.1 (Conclusion.) Steps 2.1 and 2.2 give every displayed bound with a constant depending only on $C$, $L$ and the dimension; the constants of the weaker displayed inequalities were enlarged. [step 2.1, step 2.2, given] ∎

[L1] In a chart, the Christoffel symbols of the metric-selected connection are $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\sum_dg^{ad}\bigl(\partial_bg_{cd}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}\bigr)$; equivalently, metric compatibility and torsion freedom are the identities $\partial_ag_{bc}=\sum_d(\Gamma^d{}_{ab}g_{dc}+\Gamma^d{}_{ac}g_{bd})$ and $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\Gamma^a{}_{cb}$ ([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]], [[lem-gr-connection-conditions-in-chart-components]], [[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]).

[L2] In a chart with Christoffel symbols $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$, the curvature components are $R^a{}_{bcd}=\partial_c\Gamma^a{}_{db}-\partial_d\Gamma^a{}_{cb}+\sum_e(\Gamma^a{}_{ce}\Gamma^e{}_{db}-\Gamma^a{}_{de}\Gamma^e{}_{cb})$, and $\operatorname{Ric}_{bd}=\sum_{a,c}g^{ac}R_{abcd}$, $S=\sum_{b,d}g^{bd}\operatorname{Ric}_{bd}$, $G_{ab}=\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}-\tfrac12Sg_{ab}$ ([[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]] clause (b), [[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]] clause (c)).

[L3] In coordinates, a smooth curve is a geodesic if and only if $\ddot z^k+\sum_{i,j}\Gamma^k{}_{ij}(z)\dot z^i\dot z^j=0$ on every parameter subinterval lying in the chart, where $z=x\circ\gamma$ ([[prop-coordinate-geodesic-equation]], [[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]]).

[L4] A smooth vector field $X$ on $M$ has a unique maximal local flow $\Phi:\mathcal D\to M$, $(s,p)\mapsto\gamma_p(s)$, whose fibres are the maximal integral curves; if $\Phi_s$ is defined for all $s\in\mathbb R$ and all $p$ it is a global flow ([[thm-fundamental-theorem-on-flows]], [[def-local-and-global-flow]], [[def-complete-vector-field]]).

[L5] For a smooth vector field $\xi$, the Lie derivative of the metric is $\mathcal L_\xi g=\frac{d}{ds}\big|_{s=0}\Phi_s^*g$, where $\Phi$ is the flow of $\xi$; $\xi$ is a Killing field exactly when $\mathcal L_\xi g=0$ ([[def-gr-killing-field]], [[def-lie-derivative-of-a-tensor-field]]).

[L6] On a future-directed timelike geodesic with affine parameter $s$ and constant speed $g(\gamma',\gamma')=-\lambda^2<0$, the parameter $\tau=\lambda(s-s_0)/c$ is proper time, and $U=d\gamma/d\tau$ satisfies $g(U,U)=-c^2$ ([[lem-gr-proper-time-reparametrization-and-four-velocity]] clause 3, [[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]).
[L7] In $\mathbb R^3$ the Euclidean norm satisfies $\|(w^1,w^2,w^3)\|_2^2=\sum_{i=1}^3(w^i)^2$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

1.1 (The connection vanishes.) In the inertial chart all metric components are the constants $\eta_{ab}$ by [[def-gr-minkowski-model-and-inertial-chart]] clause (a), so each partial derivative $\partial_ag_{bc}$ vanishes identically. The formula of [L1] gives $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\sum_d\eta^{ad}(0+0-0)=0$ at every point of $M$, proving (a). [L1, given, algebra]

1.2 (The coordinate fields are Killing.) Fix $a\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ and consider the map $\Psi_s(p):=p+s\,e_a$ in the identity chart, where $e_a$ is the $a$-th standard basis vector. The curve $s\mapsto\Psi_s(p)$ has coordinate derivative $e_a$ at every parameter, so it is an integral curve of $\partial_a$; it is defined for all $s\in\mathbb R$. By uniqueness of maximal integral curves in [L4], the maximal local flow of $\partial_a$ is this global flow $\Psi$. In the inertial chart the differential of $\Psi_s$ is the identity of the chart basis and the metric components are the constants $\eta_{ab}$, so the components of the pulled-back field are $(\Psi_s^*g)_{ab}(p)=g_{ab}(\Psi_s(p))=\eta_{ab}=g_{ab}(p)$ for all $p$; hence $\Psi_s^*g=g$ for every $s$. By [L5], $\mathcal L_{\partial_a}g=\frac{d}{ds}\big|_{0}\Psi_s^*g=0$, so $\partial_a$ is a Killing field. In particular $N=\partial_0$ is Killing, and $g(N,N)=-1$ by clause (c) of [[def-gr-minkowski-model-and-inertial-chart]], so it is unit timelike. This proves (c). [L4, L5, given, algebra]

2.1 (The curvature vanishes.) Substituting $\Gamma\equiv0$ into the coordinate formula of [L2] gives $R^a{}_{bcd}\equiv0$; since $\operatorname{Ric}$, $S$ and $G$ are obtained from $R^a{}_{bcd}$ and $g^{ab}$ by the contractions and products displayed in [L2], and $g^{ab}$ is the constant matrix $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, all of them vanish identically. The curvature operator vanishes because its components in the chart vanish, and a smooth tensor field all of whose components in one chart vanish is the zero field. This proves (b). [step 1.1, L2, algebra]

2.2 (Geodesics are straight lines.) Let $z:=x\circ\gamma:I\to\mathbb R^4$ be the coordinate expression of a smooth curve. By [L3] and step 1.1, $\gamma$ is a geodesic if and only if $\ddot z^k=0$ for $k=0,1,2,3$ on every parameter subinterval, that is, if and only if $z(s)=x_0+sv$ for some $x_0,v\in\mathbb R^4$; then the maximal interval is all of $\mathbb R$, because the affine expression extends to $\mathbb R$ and is again a solution. The speed is constant for every geodesic by clause 3 of [[lem-gr-parallel-transport-and-geodesic-speed]], and inserting the affine expression gives the value $g(\gamma',\gamma')=\eta(v,v)$. This proves the first two claims of (d). [step 1.1, L3, algebra]

3.1 (Future timelike geodesics and proper time.) Suppose $\eta(v,v)=-\lambda^2<0$ with $v^0>0$. By clause (c) of [[def-gr-minkowski-model-and-inertial-chart]], $\gamma$ is a future timelike curve, and by [L6] the parameter $\tau(s)=\lambda(s-s_0)/c$ is proper time, with $g(U,U)=-c^2$ for $U=d\gamma/d\tau$. This proves the third claim of (d); for (e), write $t=x^0(\gamma(s))/c=\bigl(x_0^0+sv^0\bigr)/c$, so that $d\mathbf q/dt=(c/v^0)(v^1,v^2,v^3)$ is constant; from $\eta(v,v)<0$ and $v^0>0$ we have $\sum_i(v^i)^2<(v^0)^2$, hence [L7] gives $|\mathbf w|^2=c^2\sum_i(v^i)^2/(v^0)^2<c^2$. [step 2.2, L6, L7, given, algebra] ∎

[L1] Stationary weak-field data have metric components $g_{00}=-(1+2\varepsilon\varphi)+r_{00}$, $g_{0i}=r_{0i}$ and $g_{ij}=(1-2\varepsilon\varphi)\delta_{ij}+r_{ij}$ pulled back from $U$; the metric must be Lorentzian on $\Omega$ and the spatial derivatives through order two obey the stated bounds on $K$. $$|\rho_\varepsilon-\bar\rho|\le\frac{C_2\varepsilon^2c^2}{8\pi G_NL^2}.$$

Its coordinate time range is finite. No boundedness on an unshrunk chart is assumed.
[L3] Continuous images of compact sets are compact, and compact subsets of a Hausdorff space are closed; a compact set has a finite subcover from every open cover ([[def-compact-space]]).

[L4] Absolutely continuous calculus: under the Riemannian length definition of [[thm-gr-auxiliary-complete-riemannian-metric]], the density $\sqrt{h(\gamma',\gamma')}$ is nonnegative and integrable, and its integral is additive and monotone over intervals ([[def-absolutely-continuous-function]], [[thm-absolutely-continuous-functions-have-integrable-derivatives]], [[thm-fundamental-theorem-of-calculus-for-absolutely-continuous-functions]]).

1.1 (A finite precompact causally convex cover.) For each point of $K$, choose an adapted chart and a closed coordinate ball compactly contained in it. Use its open half-radius ball as the neighborhood in strong causality [L1], obtaining a causally convex open $V$ around the point contained in that smaller ball. The collection of all such admissible $V$, charts and radii covers $K$; compactness selects finitely many members, with no choice of a family indexed by all points of $K$. Write them $V_j\subset U_j$ for $1\le j\le m$, with $U_j$ their open coordinate balls and $\overline{U_j}$ compactly contained in their respective larger charts. Define $M_j=\sup_{U_j}x_j^0-\inf_{U_j}x_j^0<\infty$, $H_j=\max_{\overline{U_j}}\|h\|_{\mathrm e,\mathrm{op}}<\infty$, and $c_j=\max\{1,\sqrt{H_j}K_j\}$. Then [L2] gives $\sqrt{h(\gamma',\gamma')}\le c_j(x_j^0\circ\gamma)'$ almost everywhere on every subarc in $U_j$. If $K$ is empty the conclusion is immediate with $L(K)=0$; henceforth use the finite cover for nonempty $K$. [L1, L2, L3, given, construct]

2.1 (The visit of a causal curve to one causally convex set is one interval.) Let $\gamma:[a,b]\to K$ be future causal and fix $j$. If $s<t$ with $\gamma(s),\gamma(t)\in V_j$, then $\gamma([s,t])\subseteq V_j$ by the defining property of $V_j$; hence the parameter set $\gamma^{-1}(V_j)$ is an interval in $[a,b]$: whenever it contains $s<t$ it contains $[s,t]$. In particular $\gamma^{-1}(V_j)$ has at most one connected component and is an interval $I_j$, possibly empty. [L1, step 1.1, given]

3.1 (Length over a compact part of one visit.) For every compact nondegenerate $[s,t]\subset I_j$, the curve image lies in $V_j\subset U_j$, so the fundamental theorem in [L4] and step 1.1 give $\int_s^t\sqrt{h(\gamma',\gamma')}\le c_j\int_s^t(x_j^0\circ\gamma)'=c_j(x_j^0(\gamma(t))-x_j^0(\gamma(s)))\le c_jM_j$. The restricted speed is integrable, since the coordinate derivatives are integrable and dominate it. The relatively open visit $I_j=\gamma^{-1}(V_j)$ need not contain its endpoints; only compact subintervals contained in $I_j$ are used in this argument. [step 2.1, step 1.1, L2, L4, given, algebra]

4.1 (Finite compact-interval cover and length sum.) The relatively open intervals $I_j$ form a finite cover of the compact parameter interval $[a,b]$. A sufficiently fine finite partition has each of its closed subintervals contained in some $I_j$, by a Lebesgue number of this cover. Assign each partition piece to the least such $j$; this requires only finitely many choices. For every index used, let $J_j$ be the closed interval from the least left endpoint to the greatest right endpoint of its assigned pieces. As $I_j$ is an interval, $J_j\subset I_j$; these finitely many compact intervals cover $[a,b]$. Step 3.1 applies on each $J_j$. The nonnegative integral over their union is at most the sum of their integrals, so the global speed is integrable and $\ell_h(\gamma)\le\sum_j\int_{J_j}\sqrt{h(\gamma',\gamma')}\le\sum_{j=1}^m c_jM_j=:L(K)<\infty$, with unused indices contributing no interval. If $a=b$ the length is zero. For an arclength-parametrized curve $\ell_h(\gamma)=b-a$, giving the second assertion. No possibly missing visit endpoint is evaluated. [step 2.1, step 3.1, L3, L4, given, algebra]

5.1 (Imprisonment form.) There is no sequence of future causal curves with images in a fixed compact $K$ and auxiliary lengths tending to infinity: each length is bounded by the same $L(K)$ from step 4.1. Equivalently, there is no family of $h$-arclength-parametrized future causal curves with images in $K$ and parameter-domain lengths tending to infinity. [step 4.1, given]

6.1 (Conclusion.) The finite causally convex cover, the interval visit estimate and the nonnegative integral bound establish both assertions, with exactly the declared calculus premises. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1] ∎

[L1] The basic limit curve lemma: for a sequence of future causal $h$-arclength-parametrized curves defined on intervals containing $[0,T]$ with initial points converging, a subsequence converges uniformly in $d_h$ on $[0,T]$ to a future causal curve satisfying (a1)-(a4) there; for intervals eventually containing $[0,n]$ for every $n$, a diagonal subsequence converges on every compact subinterval of $[0,\infty)$ and the limit is future-inextendible; the same holds in the time-reversed orientation for the past side ([[lem-gr-basic-limit-curve]] clauses (a) and (b)).

[L2] For $s<t$ inside the domain of a future causal curve $\beta$, the restriction $\beta|_{[s,t]}$ is a future causal curve from $\beta(s)$ to $\beta(t)$; hence $\beta(s)\le\beta(t)$ ([[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (a), [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] clause (c)).

[L3] Concatenation of two future causal curves at a common endpoint is a future causal curve; a curve that is both future- and past-inextendible is inextendible ([[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (d), [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] clause (d), [[lem-gr-causal-curve-conventions]] clause (d)).

[L4] $d_h$ is a metric inducing the manifold topology; for every locally absolutely continuous $\beta$ and $s<t$, $d_h(\beta(s),\beta(t))\le\ell_h(\beta|_{[s,t]})$. In particular, $h$-arclength parametrization gives the upper bound $d_h(\beta(s),\beta(t))\le t-s$, not equality in general ([[def-riemannian-distance-on-a-connected-manifold]], [[thm-riemannian-distance-is-a-metric]], [[thm-the-riemannian-distance-topology-is-the-manifold-topology]]).

[L5] In a strongly causal spacetime, causal curves with image in the compact set $K$ have $h$-length at most $L(K)$, and $h$-arclength-parametrized curves with image in $K$ have domain length at most $L(K)$ ([[lem-gr-strong-causality-compact-length-bound]]).

[L6] A uniformly Lipschitz sequence of maps from a compact interval into a compact metric space has a uniformly convergent subsequence, and its limit has the same Lipschitz bound ([[lem-gr-lipschitz-family-limit-subsequence]]).

[L7] In an adapted chart from [[lem-gr-dominating-cone-bounds]], future causal curves satisfy a uniform cone-speed estimate and the time coordinate is strictly increasing. On a compact coordinate ball, smoothness of $h$ and the local metric comparison with the Euclidean metric give constants $c,C_0>0$ such that $c|\dot x|_{\mathrm e}^2\le h(\dot\gamma,\dot\gamma)\le C_0|\dot x|_{\mathrm e}^2$. Thus the $h$-length of a causal segment contained in a smaller ball is at most $C\,\Delta x^0$, using the cone-speed estimate. To compare distance and coordinates, choose concentric coordinate balls $B_r\subset B_R$ with compact closure in the chart and $2r\le R-r$. For $y,z\in B_r$, every path staying in $B_R$ has length at least $\sqrt c\,|x(y)-x(z)|_{\mathrm e}$; every path exiting $B_R$ has initial length at least $\sqrt c(R-r)\ge\sqrt c\,|x(y)-x(z)|_{\mathrm e}$ before its first exit. Taking the infimum over paths gives $|x(y)-x(z)|_{\mathrm e}\le c^{-1/2}d_h(y,z)$. Hence a $d_h$-Lipschitz curve is locally Lipschitz in chart coordinates ([[lem-gr-dominating-cone-bounds]] clauses (a)-(c), [[thm-gr-auxiliary-complete-riemannian-metric]], [[lem-local-comparison-of-a-riemannian-metric-with-the-euclidean-metric]]).

1.1 (Common-domain reparametrization in the bounded positive case.) Suppose $0<b<\infty$. Define $\widetilde\alpha_k(t):=\alpha_k\!\left(\frac{b_k}{b}t\right),\qquad 0\le t\le b.$ Since $b_k/b\to1$, after discarding finitely many terms these curves are 2-Lipschitz for $d_h$: the arclength parametrization gives $d_h(\widetilde\alpha_k(s),\widetilde\alpha_k(t)) \le\ell_h(\widetilde\alpha_k|_{[s,t]}) =\frac{b_k}{b}|t-s|\le2|t-s|.$ Their initial points converge to $x$, and their images lie in one closed $h$-ball about $x$ of radius $2b+1$, which is compact by [L4]. Applying [L6] gives a subsequence converging uniformly on $[0,b]$ to a 2-Lipschitz map $\alpha$. The sharper inequality $d_h(\widetilde\alpha_k(s),\widetilde\alpha_k(t)) \le\frac{b_k}{b}|t-s|$ and $b_k/b\to1$ imply $d_h(\alpha(s),\alpha(t))\le|t-s|$. Uniform convergence at the endpoints gives $\alpha(0)=x$ and $\alpha(b)=z$. [L4, L6, given, construct]

1.2 (The limit is future causal.) Let $[s,t]$ be a parameter interval such that $\alpha([s,t])$ lies in a strictly convex normal set $C$. Since this image is compact and $C$ is open, uniform convergence implies $\widetilde\alpha_k([s,t])\subset C$ for all sufficiently large $k$. By [[lem-gr-causal-curve-conventions]] clause (a), each approximating causal subarc has a future-causal position vector $w_k=\exp_{\widetilde\alpha_k(s)}^{-1} (\widetilde\alpha_k(t)).$ Smoothness of the two-point inverse on $C\times C$ gives $w_k\to w=\exp_{\alpha(s)}^{-1}(\alpha(t))$; closedness of the future cone gives that $w$ is future causal or zero. Thus $\alpha$ is geodesically connectible. It is locally Lipschitz in charts by its $d_h$-Lipschitz bound and [L7], hence locally absolutely continuous. At almost every differentiability parameter $t<b$, choose a relatively compact adapted chart $U$ around $\alpha(t)$ and $h_0>0$ so $\alpha([t,t+h])\subset U$ for $0<h\le h_0$. For all sufficiently large $k$ the approximating arcs also lie in $U$ and have $h$-length $(b_k/b)h$. By [L7], $\frac{b_k}{b}h\le C\bigl(x^0(\widetilde\alpha_k(t+h)) -x^0(\widetilde\alpha_k(t))\bigr)$ for a chart constant $C$. Passing to the limit and using $b_k/b\to1$ gives $x^0(\alpha(t+h))-x^0(\alpha(t))\ge h/C.$ At differentiability points this yields $(x^0\circ\alpha)'(t)\ge1/C>0$. For small $h>0$ the position vector $\exp_{\alpha(t)}^{-1}(\alpha(t+h))$ is future causal or zero by the preceding connectibility argument; divided by $h$ it tends in coordinates to $\alpha'(t)$, because the differential of the second-variable inverse at the diagonal is the identity ([[lem-gr-joint-exponential-diffeomorphism]] clauses (b),(c)). The future cone is closed and $\alpha'$ has positive time component, so $\alpha'(t)$ is nonzero future causal almost everywhere. This proves $\alpha$ is a future causal curve and is not constant on any nondegenerate interval. [L1, L4, L6, L7, given]

1.3 (The future tail in the unbounded case.) Suppose $b=\infty$. For each fixed $T>0$, $[0,T]$ is contained in $[0,b_k]$ for all large $k$. Applying clause (b) of [L1] by diagonal extraction over integer $T$ gives a subsequence converging uniformly on every compact subinterval of $[0,\infty)$ to a future-inextendible future causal curve $\alpha^+:[0,\infty)\to M$ with $\alpha^+(0)=x$. [L1, given, choose]

1.4 (The past tail in the unbounded case.) Define $\delta_k(s):=\alpha_k(b_k+s)$ on $[-b_k,0]$. For each fixed $T>0$, $[-T,0]$ lies in $[-b_k,0]$ for all large $k$. Apply the time-reversed half-line result of [L1] and diagonalize to obtain a past-inextendible future causal curve $\alpha^-:(-\infty,0]\to M$ with $\alpha^-(0)=z$, such that $\delta_k$ converges uniformly to $\alpha^-$ on compact subintervals. A nested subsequence retains both tail limits. [L1, given, choose]

1.5 (The zero-length case.) If $b=0$, then $d_h(x,z)\le d_h(x,\alpha_k(0)) +d_h(\alpha_k(0),\alpha_k(b_k)) +d_h(\alpha_k(b_k),z)\le o(1)+b_k+o(1),$ so $x=z$. For every $t\in[0,b_k]$, $d_h(\alpha_k(t),x)\le d_h(\alpha_k(0),x)+t\le o(1)+b_k.$ Hence the curves converge uniformly on their varying domains to the constant curve at $x$. [L4, given, algebra]

1.6 (Imprisonment.) If the spacetime is strongly causal and all images lie in a compact $K$, [L5] gives $b_k\le L(K)$ for every $k$. Taking limits yields $b\le L(K)<\infty$, excluding the unbounded case. [L5, given, algebra]

2.1 (The closure relation.) Fix $t_+\ge0$ and $t_-\le0$. For all sufficiently large $k$, $t_+\le b_k+t_-$, so by [L2], $\alpha_k(t_+)\le\alpha_k(b_k+t_-)=\delta_k(t_-).$ The uniform-on-compact limits in steps 1.3-1.4 give endpoints converging respectively to $\alpha^+(t_+)$ and $\alpha^-(t_-)$. This is the stated sequential closure relation. [step 1.3, step 1.4, L2, given]

2.2 (Coincident endpoints.) If $x=z$ and $0<b<\infty$, step 1.2 gives a future causal curve $\alpha$ from $x$ to $x$ which is nonconstant on every nondegenerate interval. If $x=z$ and $b=\infty$, concatenate $\alpha^-$ and $\alpha^+$ at their common endpoint $x$. The concatenation is future causal by [L3], and is past- and future-inextendible because its respective tails are; hence it is inextendible. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 1.4, L3, given]

3.1 (Conclusion.) Clause (i) for $b>0$ is steps 1.1-1.2 and for $b=0$ is step 1.5; clause (ii) is steps 1.3, 1.4 and 2.1; clause (iii) is step 2.2; and clause (iv) is step 1.6. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 1.4, step 2.1, step 1.5, step 1.6, step 2.2] ∎

[L1] Development and subdevelopment data: $j(\Sigma)$ is a Cauchy set of $(M,g,N)$ and of $(U,g|_U,N|_U)$ ([[def-gr-development-and-data-fixing-isometry]] clause (a)5, [[def-gr-common-subdevelopment-and-corresponding-boundary]] clause (a)); consequently both are causal: a nonconstant closed causal segment can be repeated indefinitely to give a no-limit inextendible causal curve, which either misses the Cauchy set or meets it at infinitely many parameters, both impossible. The Cauchy side decomposition under the stated supplier hypotheses supplies every level relation $J^+(\Sigma)=\Sigma\sqcup I^+(\Sigma)$ holds ([[lem-gr-cauchy-set-topology-and-graph]] clause (a)).

[L2] Maximal geodesics in an open Lorentzian submanifold: for every $q$ in the Lorentzian manifold $(U,g|_U)$ and every nonzero causal $w\in T_qU$, the unique maximal geodesic $\rho:I_\rho\to U$ with $\rho(0)=q$, $\rho'(0)=w$ is future-directed causal when $w$ is, and $\rho(t)$ does not converge to any point of $U$ as $t\to\sup I_\rho$ or as $t\to\inf I_\rho$ ([[thm-gr-local-geodesics-and-exponential-map]] clause (a), [[lem-gr-maximal-geodesics-and-extension]] clause (b)).

[L3] Gluing and regularity of causal curves: the concatenation of two future causal curves at a common endpoint value is a future causal curve, and a causal curve is continuous on its interval ([[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]], [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]], [[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]).
[L4] Push-up: $p\ll q\le r$ implies $p\ll r$, so $J^+(q)\subseteq I^+(\Sigma)$ whenever $q\in I^+(\Sigma)$ ([[lem-gr-push-up-rule]] clause (a)).

[L5] Causality of causal curves: a future causal curve $\nu$ whose values at two distinct parameters coincide contains a nonconstant closed future causal curve, which is excluded by [L1]; hence $\nu$ is injective, and two distinct points of $\Sigma$ are never causally related ([[lem-gr-cauchy-set-topology-and-graph]] clause (a)). No choice principle beyond the stated supplier premises is used in this item.

[L1] The member images are open and cover $Q$, and the member maps are diffeomorphisms preserving the metric ([[lem-gr-universal-development]] clauses (c)-(d)). Exponential maps agree with their member counterparts whenever the corresponding segment stays in the member, by uniqueness of the geodesic ODE ([[thm-gr-local-geodesics-and-exponential-map]]).

[L2] Inside a member containing a prescribed point $p$, the joint exponential map $(q,v)\mapsto(q,\exp_qv)$ has a diffeomorphic restriction near $(p,0)$ with image containing a product neighborhood of $(p,p)$. Its smooth inverse gives $v(q,p)$ for every $q$ in a sufficiently small neighborhood of $p$. For each such $q$, its open fiber domain $H_q$ maps diffeomorphically onto an open subset of the member containing $p$ ([[lem-gr-joint-exponential-diffeomorphism]] clauses (a)-(c)). This argument can be performed entirely inside the member, even without using second countability of $Q$.

[L3] Countable Choice supplies one basis at each $d\in D$. Rational translated balls form a basis of the resulting Euclidean tangent space, and $D\times\mathbb Q^4\times\mathbb Q_{>0}$ is countable; every subfamily and image of this set is countable ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-countable]], [[thm-countable-union-of-countable]], [[lem-q-and-irrationals-dense-r]], [[def-topology-basis-subbasis]]).

1.1 (Countability and openness.) Use [L3] to choose the tangent bases. The family $\mathcal B$ is the image of a subset of the countable indexing set $D\times\mathbb Q^4\times\mathbb Q_{>0}$ and hence countable. Each member is open by the defining diffeomorphism condition. No arbitrary small exponential domain is fixed at a dense center. [L3, construct]

2.1 (The basis criterion.) Let $p\in O\subseteq Q$ with $O$ open. Choose a member containing $p$ and the product neighborhood of $(p,p)$ supplied by [L2]. Its first factor is an open neighborhood $V$ of $p$ in $Q$. Choose $d\in D\cap V$ by density. The inverse velocity $v(d,p)$ lies in $H_d$, where $\exp_d$ is a diffeomorphism onto an open subset of this member. Thus $H_d\cap\exp_d^{-1}(O)$ is an open neighborhood of $v(d,p)$ in $T_dQ$. In the chosen basis at $d$, select a rational translated ball $B_d(a,r)$ containing $v(d,p)$ and contained in this neighborhood by [L3]. By [L1]-[L2], the quotient exponential on this ball agrees with the member exponential and restricts to a diffeomorphism onto an open subset of $Q$, so its image belongs to $\mathcal B$ and satisfies $p\in\exp_d(B_d(a,r))\subseteq O$. [L1, L2, L3, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 (Conclusion.) Steps 1.1 and 2.1 show that $\mathcal B$ is a countable family of open sets satisfying the basis criterion. Therefore it is a countable basis and $Q$ is second countable ([[def-second-countable-space]]). [step 1.1, step 2.1, discharge-construct] ∎
